1950.note: 125 F1 at Monaco and Switzerland; 275 F1 at Belgium; 375 F1 debuted at Monza (Ascari finished 2nd after taking over Serafini's car). He was also entered in a 275 F1 for the French GP but did not start. Ferrari has no standalone 125 F1 page; the name is from Ferrari's 275 F1 page and 1950 Monaco feature.

1952.note: 500 F2 in all six European Grands Prix (Formula 2 rules); 375 Indianapolis at the Indianapolis 500 (retired, broken wheel).

1954.note: Ascari's only 1954 Ferrari start was the Italian GP at Monza (on loan from Lancia); his other 1954 starts were for Maserati and Lancia.

1956.note: Ferrari names the car 'D50'; commonly called 'Lancia-Ferrari D50' (statsf1/Wikipedia also use D50/D50A). Designed for Lancia by Jano, modified by Ferrari for 1956.

1954.note: 625 F1 in six races; 553 F1 ('Squalo') at the French GP and at the Spanish GP, which he won.

1955.note: Started 1955 with Vanwall; for Ferrari drove the 555 F1 ('Supersqualo') in the Netherlands and Italy and a 625 F1 at the British GP (shared with Castellotti).

1957.note: Ferrari and Wikipedia say the 801 raced from the 1957 Argentine GP; statsf1 lists Hawthorn's car as a D50 for Argentina and Monaco. Commonly called 'Lancia-Ferrari 801'.

1958.note: Drove a Maserati 250F (Bonnier's) at the French GP, not a Ferrari. For Ferrari: Dino 156 F2 in the Formula 2 class at the German GP, then 246 F1 at Italy and Morocco.

1959.note: Ferrari calls the 2.5-litre 1959 car '256 F1'; statsf1 and Wikipedia file it as 'Dino 246' / D246.

1960.note: Front-engined car. Ferrari says 1960 began 'still with the 256 F1'; statsf1 lists Hill's car as D246 all season and Wikipedia also calls it the 246 F1. The rear-engined 246 P F1 raced in 1960 (Ginther, Monaco), not by Hill.

1962.note: Ferrari: the same 156 F1 was used again in 1962. Hill's US GP entry was with Porsche, not Ferrari.

1963.note: statsf1 lists the 1963 '156 Aero' monocoque version at Italy, Mexico and South Africa; Ferrari names both versions 156 F1-63. Also written '156/63'.

1964.note: 158 F1 in every race, including the US and Mexican GPs entered by North American Racing Team. Ferrari's 512 F1 (flat-12, often called '1512') was raced by Bandini that year.

1965.note: Even split: 158 F1 for rounds 1-4 (South Africa, Monaco, Belgium, France) and 512 F1 for rounds 5-8 (Britain, Netherlands, Germany, Italy). Missed the last two races after being injured. 158 F1 is listed first because it started the season and scored more points. The 512 F1 is often called '1512'.

1966.note: Raced the 312 F1-66 in his two 1966 Ferrari starts (Monaco and Belgium, which he won), then left for Cooper. Often written 'Ferrari 312' (1966).

1975.note: 312 B3-74 in Argentina and Brazil; 312 T from the South African GP onwards.

1976.note: 312 T for the first three races (Brazil, South Africa, US West); 312 T2 from the Spanish GP onwards.

1977.note: Took over Lauda's car for the last two races (Canada, Japan).

1978.note: A modified 312 T2 in Argentina and Brazil; 312 T3 from the South African GP onwards.

1979.note: 312 T3 in Argentina and Brazil; 312 T4 from the South African GP onwards.

1980.note: The 126 C turbo appeared in practice but did not race in 1980.

1981.note: Ferrari names the twin-turbo car '126 CK'; the Comprex-supercharged 126 CX was tested but dropped. Often written '126C' or '126CK'.

1982.note: Raced until his fatal accident in qualifying for the Belgian GP (Zolder, 8 May 1982).

1979.note: 312 T3 in Argentina and Brazil; 312 T4 from the South African GP onwards.

1991.note: Ferrari names the 1991 car F1-91: project 642 for the first six races, replaced from the French GP by project 643 (higher nose). Wikipedia has separate '642' and '643' articles. Prost was replaced for the final race.

2002.note: Updated F2001 (sometimes 'F2001B') in Australia and Malaysia; F2002 from the Brazilian GP onwards.

2003.note: F2002 for the first four races; F2003-GA from the Spanish GP onwards. 'GA' honours Gianni Agnelli. Ferrari writes it as 'F2003-GA', 'F2003 - GA' and 'F2003 GA'.

2005.note: Interim F2004 M in Australia and Malaysia; F2005 from the Bahrain GP onwards (Ferrari). Ferrari writes 'F2004 M'; commonly 'F2004M'.

2014.note: Ferrari writes 'F14 T' (the SF15-T page also says 'F14-T').

2011.note: Launched as 'F150th Italia' and renamed; Ferrari's history pages also say 'F150° Italia'.

2014.note: Ferrari writes 'F14 T' (the SF15-T page also says 'F14-T').

2020.note: Named for Ferrari's 1000th Formula 1 Grand Prix (Mugello 2020).
Named for Ferrari's 1000th Formula 1 Grand Prix (Mugello 2020).

formula1-sf-25-launch.title: FIRST LOOK: Ferrari unveil new 2025 car after SF-25 livery reveal during F1 75 Live

125 F1.notes: Ferrari's first World Championship car; Ascari finished 2nd on its championship debut at Monaco 1950.

275 F1.notes: First unsupercharged Lampredi V12, raced from the 1950 Belgian GP at Spa.

375 F1.notes: Lampredi V12 at the 4.5-litre limit; gave Ferrari its first World Championship win (Silverstone 1951).

375 Indianapolis.notes: 375 F1 modified for the Indianapolis 500; Ascari retired with a broken wheel.

500 F2.notes: Lampredi four-cylinder F2 car; Ascari won the 1952 and 1953 titles in it.

625 F1.notes: 2.5-litre version of the Lampredi four-cylinder design, used when the 1954 rules began.

553 F1.notes: Short-stroke engine; journalists nicknamed its rounded bodywork the 'shark'.

555 F1.notes: Evolution of the 553 with coil-spring front suspension; known as 'Supersqualo' (Super shark).

D50.notes: Lancia design by Jano, taken over by Ferrari; side pontoons first held fuel, later only faired the wheels.

801 F1.notes: Ferrari evolution of the D50 with a new tubular chassis and conventional bodywork; name means 8 cylinders, Formula 1.

246 F1.notes: Dino V6 derived from the F2 project; name = 2.4 litres, 6 cylinders. Hawthorn's 1958 title car.

Dino 156 F2.notes: Formula 2 car with the first Dino V6; raced in the F2 class of the 1958 German GP.

256 F1.notes: V6 enlarged to 2.5 litres; disc brakes adopted. Still front-engined as rear-engined British cars took over.

156 F1.notes: Rear-engined; 120° V6 lowered the centre of gravity; slender nose with two angled air intakes. Won the 1961 drivers' and constructors' titles.

156 F1-63.notes: Semi-monocoque chassis and Bosch direct fuel injection.

158 F1.notes: Brought the V8 back to Ferrari; Surtees' 1964 title car.

512 F1.notes: Flat-12 engine; debuted at the 1964 US GP with Bandini.

312 F1-66.notes: Ferrari's first car for the 3-litre rules.

312 B3-74.notes: Forghieri redesign with shorter wheelbase and side radiators; took 10 poles in 1974.

312 T2.notes: Periscope airbox banned; NACA cockpit-side intakes. Lauda's 1977 title car.

312 T3.notes: Wide bodywork for Michelin radial tyres; used from the 1978 South African GP.

312 T4.notes: Ground-effect evolution of the T series; Scheckter's 1979 title car.

312 T5.notes: Last naturally aspirated flat-12 Ferrari F1 car.

126 CK.notes: First Ferrari turbo car to race; the Comprex '126 CX' version was dropped.

126 C2.notes: Postlethwaite composite chassis, lighter and stiffer; won the 1982 constructors' title.

F1-89.notes: Barnard design; first F1 car with a semi-automatic, steering-wheel-paddle 7-speed gearbox.

F1-90.notes: Evolution of the 640; Prost's five wins included Ferrari's 100th F1 victory.

F1-91.notes: Project 642, replaced from the French GP by project 643 with a higher nose.

F310.notes: Ferrari's first V10 F1 car (3 litres, 10 cylinders).

F310 B.notes: Narrower, more conventional development of the F310; Barnard's last Ferrari.

F300.notes: Byrne design for the narrow-track, grooved-tyre rules; Tipo 047 engine with an 80° vee (page text; its spec table says 90°).

F1-2000.notes: High nose; new 90° V10. Schumacher's first Ferrari title.

F2001.notes: Nicknamed the 'anteater' for its nose dropping to the front wing; won both 2001 titles.

F2002.notes: 15 wins from 17 races; new 051 engine and fused-titanium gearbox.

F2003-GA.notes: Named in honour of Gianni Agnelli.

F2004.notes: Type 655 with the 053 engine; 15 wins from 18 races.

F2004 M.notes: F2004 modified for the 2005 rules, used for the first two races of 2005.

248 F1.notes: Name = 2.4 litres, 8 cylinders; Ferrari's first V8 since the 1964 158 F1.

F2007.notes: Type 658; long wheelbase. Räikkönen's title car.

F2008.notes: Type 659; first year of the standard control unit, so no traction control.

F60.notes: Named for Ferrari's 60th F1 season; had KERS.

F10.notes: Type 661; designed for the double diffuser and the refuelling ban.

Ferrari 150° Italia.notes: Named for the 150th anniversary of Italian unification.

F2012.notes: Pull-rod suspension front and rear; stepped nose.

F138.notes: Name = 2013 + V8; the V8's last season.

SF16-H.notes: Short nose; pushrod front suspension replaced pull-rod.

SF70H.notes: Built for the wider, higher-downforce 2017 rules; the name marks Ferrari's 70th anniversary.

SF71H.notes: Project 669; first Ferrari with the halo.

SF90.notes: Raced in the Scuderia's 90th-anniversary season; narrower engine cover and 2019-rules front and rear wings.

SF1000.notes: Named for Ferrari's 1000th F1 Grand Prix (Mugello 2020).

SF21.notes: Evolution of the SF1000 on a carried-over chassis; new engine.

F1-75.notes: First ground-effect car of the 2022 rules; marks Ferrari's 75th anniversary.

SF-23.notes: Evolution of the F1-75; kept its scalloped sidepods.

SF-24.notes: Third ground-effect car; yellow and white livery details.

SF-25.notes: 71st Ferrari F1 car; darker matte red with a white band. Hamilton's first Ferrari.
